newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Cause of Israeli air crash may never be determined.
newsitem.headline: Cause of Israeli air crash may never be determined.

text.p: With no in-flight recordings and no survivors, Israeli investigators may never fully determine what caused the mid-air crash of two military helicopters, claiming the lives of 73 soldiers, analysts said on Thursday.
Security sources said an investigation team appointed by Defence Minister Yitzhak Mordechai was focusing on human error as the main factor in the worst air disaster in the country's military history.
The sources said the Sikorsky CH-53 helicopters were circling along Israel's northern border on Tuesday, waiting for permission to cross into Lebanon when they collided minutes after takeoff.

Investigators think the rotor of one of the helicopters hit the tail of the other as they flew in close formation around 7 p.m (1700 GMT), the security sources said. One of the helicopters plunged straight down while the other spiralled to the ground.
Passengers and crew in both aircraft were all killed.
Israeli helicopters turn off their lights when they enter Lebanon to avoid drawing fire from guerrillas but it was not clear whether the pilots had done so yet, security sources said.

"If the suspicion is that human error caused the crash and there's no one to question, it becomes very difficult to reach solid conclusions and recommendations," said Yisrael Yahalom, a former Sikorsky pilot who investigated the previous worst air disaster, in 1977, when a Sikorsky crashed and 54 died.
"In a collision between two vehicles, whether cars, planes, F-16s or helicopters, the main responsibility falls on the driver in the rear," said military analyst Amir Oren.
"The investigation of a collision which ends in tragedy must begin with this basic fact," he wrote in the newspaper Haaretz.
Investigators visited the site of the disaster on Wednesday in the first day of their investigation.

"I ask that you act responsibly. Don't speculate about inaccurate information that's not based on fact," Defence Minister Mordechai told reporters on Wednesday when asked about the cause of the crash.

Israeli military officials have already said weather was not a factor when the helicopters took off to take troops to Israel's 15 km (15 mile)-wide south Lebanon occupation zone. There was no flight recorder, often known as a "black box".
The death of the 73 soldiers made Tuesday the army's deadliest day since the 1973 Arab-Israeli war and plunged the Jewish state into successive days of mourning.
As rescue workers identified the bodies, army authorities released the names of more and more soldiers until it seemed nearly every Israeli could trace a connection to at least one of the victims.
Thirty-four funerals were scheduled for Thursday throughout the country. Shops and restaurants remained closed. An official period of national mourning was to last until Thursday night.
"Everyone knows at least one person who's on his way to a funeral today," said Noa Shimoni, a university student whose friend from high school was among the dead.
In Beirut, the pro-Iranian Hizbollah group fighting to expel Israel from Lebanon said the crash was an act of God.

"We consider what happened a success granted by God...I will use this occasion to express big happiness and ask our people and loved ones to pray to God and thank him," said Hizbollah deputy chief Sheikh Na'eem Qassem.
Israel's army chief Amnon Shahak said in a statement to soldiers that Israeli troops would remain in Lebanon.
